terms.gloss: appear in a dream: “I dreamt of …”
terms.grammar: what is dreamt of is the subject; the dreamer, if named, in the dative
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 383: hāc nocte in somnīs mea soror geminast germāna vīsa
Verg. A. 2.270–271: in somnīs, ecce, ante oculōs maestissimus Hector vīsus adesse mihi
terms.comment: How Latin says whom or what one dreamt of: the person vīsus est, “seemed”, to the dreamer in somnīs. For the dream itself, somniāre with an object or a clause, as Plautus’s girl says quod noctū hāc somniāvī.

phrases.english: telling a dream is for someone awake

phrases.latin: Vīn' tibi narrem quid hāc nocte somniāverim?
phrases.english: Shall I tell you what I dreamt last night?

phrases.latin: mī hau falsum ēvēnit somnium, quod noctū hāc somniāvī. — Quid somniāstī? — Ego ēloquar.
phrases.english: the dream I dreamt last night has come true! — What did you dream? — I’ll tell you.

phrases.latin: in somnīs, ecce, ante oculōs maestissimus Hector vīsus adesse mihi largōsque effundere flētūs
phrases.english: in my sleep, look, Hector seemed to stand before my eyes, full of grief and shedding floods of tears

sources: Lewis & Short: somnium · Lewis & Short: somnio
